**Ch 027, "Warned that Boutwell meant to invite no support..."**

**Ch 027, "A second quarrel, almost as fatal, worried him even more."**

Source: "another quarrel, almost as fatal to Adams as that between Fish and Sumner, worried him even more."

Draft: "A second quarrel, almost as fatal, worried him even more."

"As fatal" — fatal compared to what? In the source, the comparison is explicit: "as fatal to Adams as that between Fish and Sumner." In the draft, the Fish-Sumner quarrel has been described, so a reader can infer the comparison. "Almost as fatal" is slightly orphaned — as fatal as what? But the Fish-Sumner quarrel IS present in the draft just before this. A competent reader can infer "as fatal as the Fish-Sumner situation just described." Not a genuine confusion.

The draft keeps "Frank Walker shared this feeling, and had promised Adams for the North American Review an article on the Legal Tender Act." This is a residue of an authorized cut — Walker is on the removal list. NOT a finding.

**Ch 027: "The trail always faded and died out at the point where any member of the Administration became visible."**

In the source, this follows: "He soon knew all that was to be known; the material for his essay was furnished by the Government. Material furnished by a government seldom satisfies critics or historians... All Adams's great friends--Fish, Cox, Hoar, Evarts, Sumner, and their surroundings--were precisely the persons most mystified." The draft cuts the setup about the Congressional Investigation providing material, then jumps to "The trail always faded..." In the draft, it reads: "They went to New York to work it up, paid their respects in person to the famous Jim Fisk in his Opera-House Palace, and waited for the Congressional Investigation. The trail always faded and died out at the point where any member of the Administration became visible."

Does "the trail" parse? The Congressional Investigation was just mentioned. A reader can understand "the trail" as the investigative trail from the Congressional Investigation. This parses, if loosely. Not a genuine confusion.

**Ch 027: "He saw Sumner take possession of the Department, and he approved; he saw Sumner seize the British mission for Motley, and he was delighted"**

"the British mission for Motley" — Motley is not introduced anywhere in the draft prior to this. In the source of Ch 027, Motley appears here for the first time too (in Ch 027 source text). So this isn't a cross-chapter cut issue. But Motley has no introduction at all. Is this a missing gloss? In context, "the British mission for Motley" — a reader can understand this means Sumner got Motley appointed to the British diplomatic post. The identity of Motley matters somewhat. But then Motley reappears: "Grant took a dislike to Motley because he parted his hair in the middle." Without knowing who Motley is, a reader may be confused.

However — Motley appears in the source at the same point in Ch 027, also without prior introduction in Ch 027. The source doesn't introduce Motley in prior chapters that were cut from the draft. So this isn't a compression artifact — it was always assumed knowledge in the source. Not a finding.

**Ch 027: "Adams saw no reason why it should be denied."**

Source: "Adams repeated the story to Godkin, who made much play with it in the Nation, till it was denied. Adams saw no reason why it should be denied."

In the draft, the story about Godkin and the Nation denying the story is cut. So "it was denied" has no antecedent in the draft — there's no mention of the story being denied or of anyone denying it. "Adams saw no reason why it should be denied" — the "it" refers to a denial that was never mentioned in the draft. A reader would be genuinely confused: denied by whom? What denial?

Slightly loose, but not genuinely confusing — the reader understands they share lodgings.

**Ch 026: "like the Terebratula, as a defiance of first principles"**

The Terebratula is used as an analogy without explanation. In the source, the same paragraph uses it the same way. The phrase "as a defiance of first principles" actually provides enough context — the Terebratula is being used as an example of something that defies evolutionary first principles (i.e., it survived when it should have been extinct). The appositive "as a defiance of first principles" partially glosses it. A reader can follow the logic: Grant is like some ancient organism that shouldn't still exist. Similarly for Pteraspis: "forces of nature, energies of the prime, like the *Pteraspis*" — the context ("energies of the prime") suggests a primitive organism. 

These are authorized removal residues (Ch 023-024 geological digressions were authorized cuts). Per the rules: "Dangling references... that are direct residues of these authorized cuts... are EXPECTED and NOT findings." The Terebratula/Pteraspis callbacks are direct residues of the authorized Ch 023-024 digression cuts. NOT findings.

Frank Walker is on the authorized removal list. The draft keeps him. Since the authorized removal list says to remove him, any seam from his partial retention is an authorized-cut residue. NOT a finding.
